analysis.one_liner: Caps compensation for medical malpractice victims and forces their claims through arbitration-style panels before any lawsuit.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on March 18, 1997, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite medical malpractice rules nationwide. It would cap compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000 no matter how severe the injury, cap what a patient's lawyer can charge, require every claim to first go through an alternative dispute resolution (ADR) system instead of court, cut any award by whatever insurance or disability payments the patient already received, and make it much harder to win punitive damages — including a near-total ban on punitive damages against drug and device makers whose products were approved by the FDA. States that did not set up an approved ADR system would have a federal one imposed on them and could lose federal public health money.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, and other health care providers would face lower malpractice exposure and, supporters argued, lower insurance premiums. Medical malpractice insurers would pay out less. Drug and device makers would be shielded from punitive damages whenever their product was FDA-approved. Health insurers and disability programs would benefit because patients' awards would be reduced by payments those programs already made.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Providers, malpractice insurers, and drug makers

how_it_helps.text: Caps total noneconomic damages — compensation for pain, suffering, disfigurement, and loss of enjoyment of life — at $250,000 per injury, regardless of the number of defendants or lawsuits.
Caps the contingency fee a patient's attorney can collect on a sliding scale: 25% of the first $100,000 recovered, down to 10% above $500,000.

Requires every malpractice claim to first go through a state-certified or federally run alternative dispute resolution system before it can be filed in court, and a party who contests the panel's ruling can be forced to pay the other side's attorney fees and expert costs unless the award changes by at least 10%.
Reduces a patient's award dollar-for-dollar by any collateral source payments such as health insurance, disability, or employer wage-continuation benefits.

Bars punitive damages against a drug or device manufacturer whose product was FDA-approved or generally recognized as safe, unless the company lied to the FDA or bribed an official; it also raises the proof standard for punitive damages generally and caps them at twice compensatory damages or $250,000, whichever is greater.
Abolishes joint liability, so each defendant pays only its own percentage share of fault even if other responsible parties cannot pay.

The bill's stated findings argue that malpractice litigation drives up health care costs and malpractice insurance premiums, so the caps are framed as a cost-containment measure for the health care system.

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by medical malpractice would bear the cost: a hard $250,000 ceiling on pain-and-suffering compensation, a one-year deadline to sue after discovering an injury (three years in any case), awards reduced by insurance payouts, an added ADR layer with fee penalties for contesting it, and no punitive damages against FDA-approved products. State courts would lose their current rules because federal law would override state protections that allow higher recovery.

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 noneconomic damages cap applies no matter how catastrophic the injury or how many defendants are liable — a child with lifelong brain damage and a patient with a temporary complication would face the same ceiling.

A claim must be filed within one year of discovering the injury and never more than three years after it, which is shorter than the deadline in many states and can bar claims by patients who learn of harm late.

A patient who contests the ADR panel's decision and does not improve the award by at least 10% must pay the defendant's attorney fees and expert costs, and must post a performance bond — a financial risk that could deter injured people from ever contesting a low award.

Because awards are reduced by any insurance or disability payments the patient already received, the wrongdoer effectively escapes paying for harms those programs covered, and the patient keeps little.

States that did not get their ADR system federally certified each year would have a federal system imposed and would have to reimburse the United States for its costs, and no Public Health Service Act funds could be paid to those states, their local governments, or any entity in them.

The bill would let state agencies agree to let physician professional societies participate in practitioner licensing and review malpractice allegations, with confidentiality for the process and immunity for the society's participants — an arrangement critics would call putting the profession in charge of policing itself.

Supporters' good-faith case: they argue malpractice suits and insurance premiums raise health care costs for everyone, and that predictable caps reduce defensive medicine and keep doctors practicing in high-risk fields — benefits ordinary people would share through lower premiums and better access.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits are indirect and speculative — lower premiums for providers that might, or might not, translate into lower health care costs — while its costs are direct and fall on a narrow group of already-injured patients, who would give up uncapped jury compensation, longer filing deadlines, full attorney representation, and punitive remedies. It also reaches far beyond protecting doctors: by immunizing FDA-approved drug and device makers from punitive damages and overriding stronger state protections, it shifts the burden of corporate misconduct onto patients. A cost-containment goal can be legitimate, but this design asks the people hurt most by medical errors to finance the savings.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it simply expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Stump introduced the Health Care Liability Reform Act of 1997 on March 18, 1997, with Reps. Callahan and Everett as cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients came out ahead: they kept whatever compensation rights their state law provides, including uncapped jury awards and longer filing deadlines, and trial lawyers kept the contingency-fee system the bill would have restricted. Medical malpractice insurers, health care providers, and drug and device makers did not get the liability caps and immunity they would have gained.

for.name: Rep. Bob Stump
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Health Care Liability Reform Act of 1997.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Henry Hyde, R-IL)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — letting it die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Association of Trial Lawyers of America (plaintiffs' trial lawyers)
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal malpractice caps that would limit compensation for injured patients and restrict contingency fees.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans and no vote was ever taken, so there is no record of how the parties would have split; the bill simply died with three sponsors in committee.

industries.note: The bill's caps on noneconomic damages, attorney fees, and punitive awards would directly cut what malpractice insurers pay out on claims. Their gain is the injured patient's lost compensation.

industries.industry: Physicians, hospitals, and other health care providers
industries.note: Providers would face lower liability exposure, an extra ADR shield before any lawsuit, and looser professional oversight through industry societies' role in licensing review. Supporters argue patients benefit too through lower health care costs, but the direct effect is fewer and smaller recoveries for injured patients.
The bill would bar punitive damages against manufacturers of FDA-approved products and cap all punitive awards, sharply reducing their litigation risk when their products harm patients.

Sliding-scale fee caps, mandatory ADR, fee-shifting against claimants who don't improve an award by 10%, and performance bonds would cut contingency-fee revenue and raise the risk of taking malpractice cases. In this bill their interest runs alongside injured patients'.

Mandatory collateral source offsets would reduce patients' awards by what these programs already paid, letting them shift costs of medical harm away from defendants without losing their own recoveries from patients.
